ForgeCycle records a durable operation journal for the project it runs in
and can serve a local, read-only dashboard over that journal.

## Storage

Every user-facing command invoked inside a Git project — including failures,
and including `serve` itself — writes one operation record under the
repository's Git common directory:

```
<git-common-dir>/forgecycle/observability/operations/<operation-id>/
    meta.json       atomically replaced metadata (command, PID, start and
                    end times, exit code, workflow correlation)
    events.ndjson   append-only event stream
    debug/          raw adapter output, only with debug: true
<git-common-dir>/forgecycle/observability/notifications.ndjson
                    append-only notification history (see "Notification
                    history" below)
```

The location is shared by the project's worktrees, absent from `git
status`, and available before `forgecycle init` creates `.forgecycle`.
Directories use mode `0700` and files use mode `0600`. The canonical common
directory is resolved and verified before anything is written or served.
Commands invoked outside a Git project are not recorded.

Two identifiers correlate records:

- **Operation ID** — one CLI invocation, with command, times, PID, exit
  code, and events. The command is the full name, such as `task run`,
  `roadmap decompose`, or `doctor`, and its slug is part of the ID
  (`20261025T153000Z-task-run-1a2b3c4d`).
- **Workflow ID** — one task run, roadmap run, or `roadmap decompose`
  lifecycle. `task run`, `task approve`, `task reject`, `task resume`,
  `task abandon`, and `task clean` reference the task run
  ID; `roadmap run`, `roadmap resume`, `roadmap status`, and
  `roadmap abandon` reference the roadmap run ID; `roadmap decompose` mints
  its own workflow ID before the model call; `task status` references the
  task run it inspected.

A roadmap run's operations emit `phase_started` for each task
(`task FC02 (2/3) on <sha>`), `state_changed` for each integration, stop, and
completion, and `artifact_written` for its `roadmap.json` snapshot and
`result.md`. Its task runs are child processes with their own operations and
workflows, so each task run's turns and events stay with its own workflow,
including its `auto-resume after <stop-kind>` events. A
workflow is of kind `roadmap-run` when
`.forgecycle/roadmap-runs/<id>/state.json` exists, `run` for a task run, and
`decompose` otherwise.
`roadmap decompose` and `roadmap questions` record their Decomposer turns in
the `decomposing` phase; task runs use `planning`, `building`, and
`reviewing`.

Event kinds: `command_started`, `command_finished`, `phase_started`,
`candidate_started`, `agent_activity`, `candidate_finished`,
`validation_failed`, `repair_started`, `handoff_accepted`, `artifact_written`,
`state_changed`, `heartbeat`, and `diagnostic`. Candidate events carry the
normalized failure category and retryability already used by adapters. A
handoff that fails validation emits `validation_failed` for both the initial
attempt and the repair attempt, with `field` naming the first failing
location (`tests[1].command`, `front_matter`, `metadata`, `sections`). Each
failure also appends a `protocol_error` line to the run's `events.log`
(`detail=invalid_handoff` or `detail=invalid_handoff_repair`, which marks a
failed repair, followed by `validation_field=<path>`). The summary is the
field-specific validation error. A stored handoff emits `handoff_accepted`,
with category `first_pass` or `repair` and a summary naming the normalizations
and filled facts. A repaired handoff also appends `detail=repair_success`, and
a normalized one appends `outcome=normalized … detail=normalized(<rules>)`.
Quota cooldowns appear as `diagnostic` events with category `quota_cooldown`,
and in `events.log` as `outcome=quota_cooldown … detail=until(<time>)` when a
cooldown starts and `outcome=skipped … detail=quota_cooldown_until(<time>)`
when a candidate is skipped. Ignored files that a Planner or Reviewer turn created appear
as `new_ignored_files` diagnostics. A configured governing file that exists
in the repository but not in the run worktree is reported as a
`missing_instructions` diagnostic when `task run` or `task resume` starts.
Gates appear as `gate` diagnostics in the `reviewing` phase. Each
gate run emits one when it starts and one with its result. A stored result
reused for the same HEAD emits one, and a gate failure that stops the run
emits one. The gate's own output is in its log under `RUN_DIR/gates/<head>/`,
not in the journal.
Processes an agent turn left running in the worktree or in the task-run
directory, which holds its evidence directory, and which ForgeCycle stops
when the turn ends on Linux and macOS, appear as
`leftover_processes` diagnostics naming each process and its directory, in
`events.log` as `outcome=leftover_processes … detail=stopped=<n>`, and on
the console as `forgecycle: warning: stopped <n> process(es) the <role> turn
left running: pid <pid> (worktree): …; pid <pid> (task-run directory): …`.
Retry sweeps over retryable failures are announced with `diagnostic` events. While a command runs, a heartbeat event is
written every 30 seconds, separate from genuine agent activity.

### Candidate-quality summary

```
forgecycle observe --summary [--workflow ID] [--json]
```

Aggregates the journal per candidate: invocations, first-pass valid handoffs,
validation failures and the most frequent failing field, repairs and repaired
successes, handoffs ForgeCycle normalized, quota cooldowns, and mean
invocation duration. Use it to decide routing (for example, whether a model
still belongs in `building`) without reading raw debug logs. `--workflow`
restricts the summary to one run or decomposition.

### Evidence

Each turn's `EVIDENCE_DIR` is `<run-dir>/evidence/turn-NNN/`, where
`<run-dir>` is `.forgecycle/task-runs/<task-run-id>/`. Agents write
logs, reports, and probes there instead of `/tmp`. `task clean` keeps evidence with
the run's other artifacts. The dashboard lists each turn's evidence files by
name; they are not served over HTTP.

`task clean` removes a run's worktree but leaves the observability history
intact. Runs created before observability exist are shown from their
existing `state.json`, handoffs, and `events.log`, labeled as a partial
timeline; no old command or agent events are invented. Existing
`state.json` and immutable handoffs remain authoritative for run state and
results — the journal explains the path to those results.

## Privacy

The journal never stores raw prompts, provider output, credentials,
feedback content, or arbitrary CLI argument strings. Summaries are
sanitized and bounded. Raw stdout/stderr stays behind the existing
`debug: true` setting, is written under the operation's private `debug/`
directory (a durable location for `roadmap decompose`, whose prompt workspace is
disposable), and is never served over HTTP. With `debug: true`, each run turn
also retains the exact turn and repair prompt files it sent to candidates
under the run's `debug/` directory, as the post-mortem record of what the CLI
told the model. The notification history stores run IDs, task labels, stop
kinds and details, next commands, command names, and operation IDs, but
never the free-text stop reason. An observability or notification history
write failure is reported as a `forgecycle: warning:` diagnostic and never
changes the primary command result, its output, or its exit code.

## The dashboard

`forgecycle serve` starts a separate, read-only HTTP process:

```
forgecycle serve [--port N] [--listen ADDR] [--public-url URL] [--no-auth] [--open]
```

- Binds to `127.0.0.1` by default, validates the `Host` header, and starts
  only on explicit request. `--port 0` (the default) picks an available port.
- `--listen ADDR` binds to another IP address instead, such as `0.0.0.0`
  (every IPv4 address), `::`, or one interface address, so other machines
  can open the dashboard.
  A host name is a usage error (exit 64). Beyond loopback the `Host` check
  also admits any IP address and this machine's names (its hostname, the
  hostname's first label, and that label with `.local`); any other name is
  refused, which keeps DNS rebinding out. `serve` prints the loopback URL,
  then one `Dashboard on the network:` URL per network address of the
  machine when listening on every address (the address of the default
  route first, so a Docker bridge or VPN address does not lead), then a
  warning.
- Beyond loopback, `serve` also prints the first network URL (or the
  bound interface address) as a QR code, so a phone or tablet can open the
  dashboard without typing the token. It draws the code with Unicode half
  blocks, black on white, only when stdout is a terminal; logs and pipes
  get the URL lines alone. If the machine has no network address, it says
  so instead. The dashboard's header always has a share button that opens a
  dialog with the entry URL (with the access token; the first network URL,
  or the loopback one on loopback) and a Copy button. Beyond loopback the dialog also shows the
  same QR code, a selector when there are several
  network addresses (preset to the one the browser used), and the URL with
  a Copy button. The QR code holds the access token, like every printed
  URL, so anyone who scans it can read the project; the page shows it only
  when asked. The codes come from a small built-in encoder
  (`internal/qr`), not a third-party library. The dashboard
  is plain HTTP, so the token and cookie cross the network in clear text;
  use it only on a network you trust, or put a TLS reverse proxy (which
  sets `Host` to an allowed value, or use `--public-url`) or an SSH tunnel
  in front of it. Other machines do not get browser notifications, because
  a plain-HTTP network address is not a secure context.
- `--public-url URL` names the address other devices use: a reverse
  proxy's `https://forge.example.com`, a DNS name with a port
  (`http://forge.example.com:8080`), or a bare domain (`forge.example.com`),
  which means plain HTTP on the port `serve` binds. It takes a scheme and
  host (and optional port) only; a path, query, fragment, user info, or
  another scheme is a usage error (exit 64). Its host passes the `Host`
  check, case-insensitively and with or without a trailing dot; no other
  name is added, and on loopback IP literals stay refused. `serve` prints
  `Dashboard at the public URL:` and draws its QR code, and the share
  dialog's QR code and Copy button offer it alone, instead of the network
  addresses. A reverse proxy on this machine can reach a loopback `serve`,
  so `serve` only notes that; a bare domain needs `--listen` too. `--open`
  still opens the loopback URL. An `https` public URL is a secure context,
  so browser notifications work on the devices that open it.
- `--no-auth` serves every request without the access token: every printed
  and shared URL is the plain page, `/auth` redirects to `/` without setting
  a cookie, and the manifest starts at `/`. `serve` warns that anyone who
  can reach the dashboard (on loopback, any user or program on this
  machine) can read the project. The `Host` check still applies: it, not
  the token, stops another website from reading the dashboard through your
  browser by DNS rebinding.
- Prints a one-time URL containing a random per-server access token
  (unless `--no-auth`). Visiting it exchanges the token for an HttpOnly, `SameSite=Strict`
  cookie and redirects to a clean URL. CORS is not enabled and no remote
  scripts are loaded.
- `--open` hands that URL to the platform opener (`open` on macOS,
  `xdg-open` on Linux, `rundll32` on Windows) once the server is
  listening. If the opener fails, a warning is printed and the server keeps
  running; open the printed URL manually.
- The page shows the project name (the base name of the repository root)
  in its header and browser tab title.
- Serves the project resolved at startup and never follows user-supplied
  repository paths. HTTP requests are never recorded as command events.
- Does not expose approval, resume, or other mutation routes. Attention
  items and notifications show the next command; they never run it.

Read endpoints:

| Endpoint | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/operations` | paginated command history with filters for live, command (the full name, for example `task run`), outcome, and workflow |
| `GET /api/operations/{id}/events` | retained events |
| `GET /api/operations/{id}/stream` | Server-Sent Events with reconnectable event IDs |
| `GET /api/workflows` | the 100 most recent workflows, each with its turns, and `plans`: the `roadmap.json` manifest of every plan directory they name (see "Turns and plans") |
| `GET /api/workflows/{id}` | run or decomposition summary, operations, turns, and authoritative run state |
| `GET /api/workflows/{id}/task` | a task run's task snapshot (`task.md` in its run directory), as Markdown |
| `GET /api/plans/task?plan=&task=` | the Markdown file a plan's `roadmap.json` names for one task id |
| `GET /api/workflows/{id}/turns/{n}` | one turn: its handoff's front matter, sections, and stored text, its journal events, its evidence file names, and a Builder turn's changed files and commit subject |
| `GET /api/workflows/{id}/turns/{n}/diff?path=` | the diff of one file the turn changed (bounded to 1 MiB) |
| `GET /api/artifacts/{workflow}/{artifact}` | strict allowlist of recorded generated artifacts |
| `GET /api/attention` | runs that need an operator (see "Needs attention and notifications") |
| `GET /api/attention/stream` | Server-Sent Events: the attention snapshot on connect and on every change, the newest 50 notifications (`event: notifications`) on connect and on every change, and `event: closed` when `serve` stops |
| `GET /api/notifications` | the notification history, newest stop first, paged with `offset` and `limit` (default 50, at most 200) |
| `GET /api/candidates` | the per-candidate quality figures `observe --summary` prints, over the whole journal (recomputed at most every 10 seconds), and the active quota cooldowns |
| `GET /manifest.webmanifest` | the web app manifest: project name, standalone display, the icons, and the token entry URL as its start URL |
| `GET /favicon.svg`, `/apple-touch-icon.png`, `/icon-192.png`, `/icon-512.png` | the icons, served without the session cookie (they hold no project data) but behind the `Host` check |
| `GET /api/share` | `{"remote": bool, "public": bool, "auth": bool, "url": string, "urls": [{"url", "svg"}]}`: the entry URL to copy (the public URL, else the first network URL, else the loopback one), whether other machines can open the dashboard (it listens beyond loopback or names a `--public-url`), whether a public URL is named, whether the token is required, and the entry URLs other machines can open, each with its QR code as SVG (only the public URL when one is named; none on loopback without one) |

Artifact serving resolves only ids recorded by `artifact_written` events;
filesystem paths, traversal, and symlink escapes are rejected. A task file is
served only as the entry a valid `roadmap.json` inside the repository names
for the requested task id, and a task snapshot only from the run directory
of a valid run id; both refuse a path that leaves the repository or
traverses a symlink. A turn's
handoff is read from the run directory by its numbered name
(`NNN-planner-plan.md`, `NNN-builder-result.md`, `NNN-reviewer-review.md`,
and `NNN-human-feedback.md`: feedback is the operator's own direction and is
shown as its own turn, so the dashboard explains why the next turn changed
course; the journal still never stores it). A
diff is served only for a path in the turn's own change list, computed with
Git from the turn's commit range (or, while a Builder turn runs, from the
run worktree against the previous head); any other path is a 404.

### Turns and plans

A turn is one numbered handoff joined with the journal events of the agent
that wrote it. The journal opens each turn with `phase_started` and the
summary `turn N` (`planning`, `building`, or `reviewing`) and closes it with
the `artifact_written` that names the stored handoff; a turn interrupted and
resumed in the same role spans both operations. A turn number names the
next handoff, so a turn that stopped without one gives its number to the
turn that follows: an interrupted Builder turn 2 resumes into reviewing as
Reviewer turn 2, which is a new turn with its own start and activity. A decomposition has one Decomposer turn per
`decomposing` phase. Each turn reports its role, its outcome (the handoff's
`status` or `verdict`; `running` while a live operation works on it;
`feedback` for human feedback; `failed` with the candidate's failure
category when no handoff was stored), the candidate that wrote it with the
adapter and model recorded when the turn ran, when it started (its latest
`phase_started`: a Reviewer turn's gates count before any agent starts, and
a resumed turn does not count the time the run was stopped) and how long it
took, whether a repair attempt produced it, and for a
Builder turn the files, added lines, and deleted lines of its commit (from
the previous accepted head, or the run base, to its own head). Handoffs stay
authoritative: an outcome is read from the handoff, never inferred from
events.

`plans` lists each plan directory the workflows name whose `roadmap.json`
is readable inside the repository: its title (the first heading of the
manifest's source plan, else the directory name), its tasks in manifest
order with their dependencies, and its `decisions.md` sections with their
recommended and given answers. A roadmap run's workflow adds `decisions`
from its own copy: the answers it ran with, plus the `H`
decisions given to its stopped task runs. Once a roadmap run exists, the
plan view shows that copy.

### Layout

The page has two panels and a status bar.

The left panel has five views, chosen from the rail on its left:

- **Now** is what a glance asks: "Needs you" lists the runs that need an
  operator, each with its stop, its next command with a Copy button, and
  what that command does; "Running now" lists every live agent with its
  task, role, candidate, elapsed time, and liveness (for example "Heartbeat
  overdue"); "Recently finished" lists the six latest finished turns with
  their outcome and when they ended. Every row opens its item. A phone opens
  on Now; every other screen opens on Work.
- **Work** is the planned work as a tree. Each plan is a section whose header
  stays pinned while you scroll, with a progress bar of one segment per task.
  Under it come the decomposition and the manifest's tasks in order, then
  any task run of the plan the manifest does not name; under each task, the
  turns of its latest task run, and earlier attempts as their own nodes.
  Task runs outside a decomposed plan are listed newest first under
  "Standalone task runs". A task row shows its status, one small mark per
  turn colored by role (hollow when the turn set the task back: changes
  requested, partial, blocked, failed), its total added and deleted lines,
  and its elapsed time. A turn row shows its number, role, candidate, lines
  changed, outcome, and duration. "Needs attention" is pinned above the
  tree. The tree can be filtered by text (`/`), narrowed to active or
  attention runs, collapsed, and walked with the arrow keys; "Locate"
  scrolls to the open item. The tree remembers which nodes are open in the
  browser's local storage. As the panel narrows, candidates and then turn
  marks and line counts are hidden before names are cut.
- **Notifications** is the notification history (see "Notification
  history") and holds the browser notification switch.
- **Commands** is the command history with a text filter: each command with
  its workflow, start time, duration, and exit code. Exit codes 20 and 21
  are stops, not failures.
- **Candidates** has one card per candidate from `/api/candidates`: the
  roles, adapter, and model it ran with in the listed workflows, its
  invocations, first-pass valid handoffs, repairs, normalizations, quota
  stops, mean duration, most frequent failing validation field, and an
  active cooldown. "Show its turns" filters the work tree to it.

Outside the phone layout, clicking the open view's icon collapses the left
panel so the right panel takes the width; clicking any view icon, or the
panel button at the foot of the rail, opens it again. Filtering, the
attention bell, and "Locate" reopen it on Work. A splitter line with a grip
in its middle sits between the panels; drag it, or focus it and press the
left and right arrow keys, to resize the left panel. The browser remembers
whether it is collapsed and how wide it is.
The right panel's views fill its width; Markdown paragraphs and lists wrap
at a readable line length.

The right panel opens the selected item in tabs: one click opens a preview
tab (in italics) that the next click replaces, a double-click keeps it. The
address follows what is shown, so a reload or a copied link opens the same
item, tab, and view, and a notification reopens its run:

- the path names the item: `/workflows/<id>` for a task run, a
  decomposition, or a plan's roadmap run, `/workflows/<id>/turns/<n>` for a
  turn, and `/?plan=<dir>` or `/?plan=<dir>&task=<id>` for a plan or task no
  run has started;
- `tab` names the item's sub tab (for example `activity` or `changes`), and
  `file` the file open in its Changes or Files tab;
- `view` names the left panel's view when it is not the screen's default
  (Work, or Now on a phone).

The page refreshes every few seconds by changing only what changed, so the
scroll position, a touch scroll in progress, and a text selection survive
it.

On a phone the dashboard shows one pane at a time. The smallest supported
screen is an iPhone 16 (393 x 852 CSS pixels), in portrait and landscape. The
phone layout applies below 700 pixels wide, or below 500 pixels tall on a
touch screen, which is a phone on its side:

- The views (Now, Work, Notifications, Candidates, Commands) are a tab bar with
  labels at the bottom, or a rail on the left in landscape. A tap shows that
  view's list.
- Tapping an item opens it full screen under a header with a Back button and
  its name, in place of the tabs. Each opened item adds a browser history
  entry, so the Back button, the browser's Back, and the swipe-back gesture
  return to the previous item and then to the list. The list keeps its
  scroll position for each view.
- A link to an item opens it, and Back then shows the list. While the
  list shows, the address is `/` (with `?view=` for a view other than
  Now), so a reload shows the list.
- Tree rows show the status, id, name (up to two lines), and time; turn
  marks and line counts are left to the item's own view. Sub tabs scroll
  sideways, breadcrumbs stack as a path, and the status bar keeps only the
  connection and the running agents.
- Diff lines wrap by default; "Wrap lines" in the Changes card switches
  between wrapping and sideways scrolling on every layout, and the browser
  remembers the choice.
- The layout uses the visible height (`100dvh`) and keeps clear of the
  notch, the Dynamic Island, and the home indicator.

On a touch screen (phone or tablet) rows and tabs are at least 44 pixels
tall and buttons at least 36, a tree chevron's tap area reaches into the
indent, and inputs use 16-pixel text so iOS Safari does not zoom in when
they get focus. Without hover there are no tooltips, so the "Needs
attention" cards show what each next command does as text.

Copy buttons work on a network address too. A plain-HTTP address is not a
secure context, so browsers withhold the Clipboard API there; the page then
falls back to the browser's older copy command.

The page has a favicon, a home-screen icon, and a web app manifest, so a
phone can add the dashboard to its home screen and open it full screen. The
icons hold no project data and are served without the session cookie; the
manifest names the project, so it needs the session. Its start URL is the
token entry URL, so the home-screen app signs in on every launch even where
it does not share the browser's cookies. The token is new for every
`forgecycle serve`, so the home-screen icon stops working once serve
restarts: scan the new QR code and add it again. With `--no-auth` the start
URL is `/` and the icon keeps working across restarts. `scripts/icons.sh`
regenerates the PNG icons from `internal/server/assets/icon.svg`.

Between 700 and 900 pixels wide the work panel stacks above the detail. Every
layout opens a newly selected item at its top; a refresh of the same item
keeps the scroll position.

- **A turn** shows a breadcrumb (plan, task, turn), the role, the candidate
  with its adapter and model, then on the next line its revision range (or
  "uncommitted changes" while a Builder works), when it started ("started
  15m ago"), and its timing ("running for 2h 23m 14s" while it runs, "took
  12m 12s" once it ends), and a strip of the
  run's turns (`[` and `]` step through them). Its tabs:
  - *Handoff*: the turn's conclusion first, in its own words (the Planner's
    scope; the Builder's summary, commit, and the open findings it
    addresses; the Reviewer's rationale and follow-up instructions), then
    what it read, what it wrote, and what came next. Then the plan's
    criteria and required tests, the Builder's tests, or the Reviewer's
    criteria (with how each moved since the previous review), independent
    test results next to what the Builder reported, and findings tagged
    new, still open, or resolved here. The full handoff follows with an
    outline.
  - *Working on*, instead of Handoff while a turn runs: its latest action,
    the instructions it follows (the last review's follow-up instructions or
    the plan's Builder instructions), the findings it must resolve, and the
    files it has touched so far.
  - *Activity*: the turn's journal events on a time track and as a timeline,
    a tool's start and finish merged into one row with its duration and
    result, filterable by kind.
  - *Changes* (Builder): the changed files and the diff of the selected one.
  - *Evidence*: the turn's evidence file names. *Raw*: the stored handoff.
  - A human feedback turn shows the feedback and the turn that read it;
    the turn after it lists it among what it read.
- **A task run** shows its id and task file, then on the next line its
  number of turns, when it started ("started 2h ago"), and how long its
  turns worked in total ("worked 45m 12s"; the time a run sat stopped
  between turns is not counted). Below come its stop with the next command
  and the phase a resume re-enters, a Planning → Building → Reviewing → Done stepper, the
  turns sized by duration, and facts: run state, live operation status,
  branch, base revision, latest head, policy, approval policy, the
  candidates of each role, quota cooldowns, and the roadmap run. Its *Task*
  tab shows the task snapshot its agents read, rendered. Its other tabs show
  each criterion by review and each required test by turn, every finding's
  status across reviews, and its files.
- **A task no task run has started** shows what it waits for and its task
  file from the plan, rendered and refetched every refresh.
- **A plan** shows its tasks with status and integrated head, its roadmap
  run (state, integration branch and head, stop and next command), and its
  decisions: the roadmap run's copy once one exists, else the plan's file.
  Its Stats tab aggregates all task run attempts under the plan: completion
  count and percentage and its timeline, active turn time by role and task
  with each role's share, Builder commits and
  changed lines, review rounds, first-review approvals, latest-review
  criteria/tests/findings, validation failures, repairs, candidate failures,
  and quota stops. First-review approvals, criteria satisfied, tests passed,
  and candidate failures show counts and percentages with explicit
  denominators; percentages with no samples show a dash. Remaining work is
  estimated as the number of non-skipped, unfinished tasks times the median
  active time of completed tasks, less active time
  already spent on the current task's latest run (up to one median task). The finish date adds
  that duration to the current time only while the roadmap is running; it
  assumes sequential, continuous execution and excludes future human pauses
  and failures. Before a completed task has recorded time, no ETA is shown.
  A partial journal labels potentially incomplete figures. Token usage and
  cost are unavailable because the journal does not record them. The Files tab
  shows the roadmap run's recorded files.
- **A decomposition** shows the tasks it wrote, its Decomposer's activity,
  the plan's decisions, and the files it wrote.

Handoffs, feedback, and Markdown files are rendered by
`internal/server/assets/markdown.js`: front matter, headings, paragraphs,
emphasis, strikethrough, code spans and blocks, block quotes, nested and
task lists, tables with column alignment, rules, and links. The page never
loads or runs agent content: raw HTML is shown as text, an image is shown as
a link to it, only `http`, `https`, and `mailto` links become clickable (they
open in a new tab), and a relative link, which names a repository file the
server does not serve, shows its target on hover.

The Files tab lists the workflow's artifacts (`artifacts` in
`/api/workflows/{id}`), oldest first, with the candidate and phase that
wrote each, and shows the selected one through `/api/artifacts`: Markdown
rendered, JSON indented. A handoff links to its turn.

Stop reason, stop kind, next action, and resume target come from the same
stop report `forgecycle status` prints, so an approval gate reads
`approval_gate (after_planning)` with `forgecycle task approve <id> (human
decision)` and resumes into `building (after approve)`, and a task run left
in an active state with no live process reads `interrupted` with
`forgecycle task resume <id>`. A roadmap run reads `interrupted` with
`forgecycle roadmap resume <id>` when no process advances it while it is
`running`. `/api/workflows/{id}` returns a roadmap run's tasks as
`roadmap_tasks` (`id`, `status`, `task_runs`, `head_revision`), with
`integration_branch`, `integration_head`, `stop_kind`, `next_action`, and
`decisions`.

The status bar shows whether the page reaches the server, how many agents
are running, and active quota cooldowns. The page polls
`/api/workflows` every four seconds and refetches a running turn's detail;
a finished turn's detail is fetched once.

When the page loses `serve`, a red banner under the title bar says which
of three things happened, and the page stops looking live: it is greyed
out, spinners and running clocks stop, the status bar shows the time of
the last update instead of running agents, and the tab title starts with
`Offline`.

- **forgecycle serve was stopped.** Ctrl-C or SIGTERM makes `serve` send
  `event: closed` on every open attention stream before it shuts down, so
  the page says so at once.
- **Cannot reach forgecycle serve.** A network error or an HTTP error
  other than 401, for example a crashed `serve` or a phone that left the
  network. A dropped attention stream triggers an immediate check, and
  the page retries every four seconds and recovers by itself.
- **This dashboard session has ended.** `serve` answers 401: it was
  restarted, and each start makes a new access token. Opening the URL the
  new `serve` printed, in any tab, sets the cookie for this tab too, and
  the page reconnects.

A tab that becomes visible again, such as a phone waking up, checks at
once.

### Needs attention and notifications

A run needs attention when it has a stop report and no live process will act
on it: a task run that is paused, blocked, failed, or at an approval gate, a
task run or roadmap run that is `interrupted`, or a stopped or failed roadmap
run. A stop that `--auto-resume` is about to resume is never listed, because
that process keeps the run's process lock while it resumes. A stop is listed
once its `state.json` has stood unchanged for 2 seconds with no process
holding the lock. A roadmap run stopped because one of its task runs stopped
is folded into that task run's item while the task run is listed, since the
operator resolves the task run first. The list comes from the same code as
`forgecycle status`.

The Work view pins these runs under "Needs attention", human decisions
first, with the stop kind, how long ago it stopped, and the first next
command (hover it for what it does); a click opens the run. The bell in the
header counts them and narrows the tree to them, and the tab title shows
the count, for example `(2) myproject · ForgeCycle`.

Browser notifications are opt-in per browser. "Enable alerts" in the
Notifications view asks for the browser's permission; the prompt only
appears after that click. When enabled, each new stop shows one notification
titled with the project, the task, and whether it needs a decision, and its
body is the stop kind and next command. Clicking it opens the run in the
dashboard. The
stop reason is left out because notifications appear on lock screens and in
notification history. A new stop of the same run notifies again; reloading
the page or opening a second tab does not. Stops that already existed when
notifications were first used are listed but do not pop up.

Notifications only fire while a dashboard tab is open: the page receives
`/api/attention/stream` and shows them itself. There is no service worker
and no Web Push, which would need a third-party push service. The loopback
URL `forgecycle serve` prints first is a secure context, which the browser
Notifications API requires; so is an `https` `--public-url`.

### Notification history

The Notifications view lists every stop that needed an operator, newest
first: when it started, the same title as its browser notification, its stop
kind, and whether it is still **open** or was **resolved**, with when, by
which command, and the run's state afterwards; a click opens the run. For example, "resolved
10:30 by task approve → building". Rows raised since this browser last left
the dashboard are marked **new**; that mark is kept in the browser's local
storage and is the only per-browser part. "Show older" pages through the
rest.

The history is recorded by ForgeCycle itself, not by the dashboard, so it
covers stops that happened while no dashboard was running:

- The command that owns a run (`task run`, `task resume`, `task approve`,
  `task reject`, `task abandon`, and the `roadmap`
  commands) appends a `raised` record when it releases the run with a stop
  report. A stop that `--auto-resume` resumes in the same process is never
  recorded.
- The command whose state save clears an open stop appends a `resolved`
  record naming itself and the run's new state. `prune --runs` resolves the
  stops of the runs it deletes as `deleted`.
- A killed process records nothing. The next command that takes the run
  records the stop it finds, such as `interrupted`, as detected later, dated
  from when the run last changed. Until then the dashboard lists the stop
  from the live attention snapshot as "not recorded yet".
- An open entry whose run no longer has that stop, although no command
  resolved it (its state file was removed by hand), reads "no longer
  stopped".

The log is `notifications.ndjson` next to `operations/`, one JSON record per
line (`schemas/notification-log.schema.json`). A roadmap run stopped
because of its task run has its own entry next to the task run's. Past 1 MiB
the log is compacted to every open entry and the newest 500 resolved ones.
`forgecycle serve` only reads it, and `GET /api/notifications` returns the
merged list with `recorded`, `stale`, `late`, `raised_*`, and `resolved_*`
fields.

### Liveness

The dashboard keeps three timestamps distinct: last command heartbeat,
last provider output, and last normalized agent action. A quiet provider is
not automatically stuck. If a command exits without a finish event, the
server checks its PID and heartbeat and labels it `ended without a recorded
result` or `heartbeat overdue`; it never asserts success, failure, or a new
protocol state. Candidate events show the configured timeout, including
`none` when `timeout_seconds` is zero.

## Adapter activity capability

Adapter output is consumed while the process runs and teed to the capture
path, so final-response extraction and debug behavior are unchanged.
Adapters translate output into a small common vocabulary: `search`,
`file_read`, `tool_started`, `tool_finished`, `message`, and
`provider_status`.

| Adapter | Live activity |
| --- | --- |
| `opencode` | NDJSON text and tool events |
| `codex` | `--json` item events |
| `claude` | unavailable — single JSON document at exit |
| `agy` | unavailable — single JSON document at exit |

For adapters without incremental events the dashboard states that live
agent activity is unavailable and still shows heartbeat and phase progress.
Actions are never inferred from silence, and a model's private reasoning is
never exposed as an observable event. Line length, event payload size, and
retained activity volume are bounded so large output cannot exhaust memory
or disk.

The streaming parsers map only event shapes exercised by the supported CLI
versions and the test fakes; unrecognized JSON events are skipped rather
than guessed at. When upgrading a supported CLI, re-verify its event
shapes against these parsers before relying on new activity types.
